claim: ApbE is an enzyme that catalyzes post-translational flavinylation by transferring the FMN portion of FAD to a conserved [S/T]GA[S/T]-like sequence motif
source: ApbE enzyme, which transfers the FMN portion of a substrate FAD molecule to a conserved [S/T]GA[S/T]-like sequence motif (flavinylated amino acid in bold) (Figure 1A; Bertsova et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertsova et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1A showing the reaction mechanism

claim: The ApbE-catalyzed phosphoester bond irreversibly links the FMN ribitylphosphate group to a serine/threonine hydroxyl side chain
source: The resulting phosphoester bond irreversibly links the FMN ribitylphosphate group to a serine/threonine hydroxyl side chain in the FMN-binding domain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the chemical nature of the flavinylation reaction

claim: Approximately 50% of bacterial genomes encode extracytosolic flavinylation components
source: This analysis provides evidence that ~50% of the bacterial (15,095) and ~4% of archaeal (63) genomes possess extracytosolic flavinylation components (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational analysis of 31,910 prokaryotic genomes searching for ApbE and FMN-binding domains with signal peptides

claim: Approximately 4% of archaeal genomes encode extracytosolic flavinylation components
source: This analysis provides evidence that ~50% of the bacterial (15,095) and ~4% of archaeal (63) genomes possess extracytosolic flavinylation components (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational analysis of 31,910 prokaryotic genomes searching for ApbE and FMN-binding domains with signal peptides

claim: Extracytosolic flavinylation components are broadly distributed across bacterial life but underrepresented in Cyanobacteria and the candidate phyla radiation
source: A phylogenetic analysis of the resulting dataset reveals that extracytosolic flavinylation components are broadly distributed across bacterial life – though strikingly underrepresented in Cyanobacteria and the candidate phyla radiation (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic reconstruction showing distribution patterns across bacterial phyla

claim: DUF2271 is a novel ApbE substrate that contains a conserved [S/T]GA[S/T] motif
source: Consistent with DUF2271 serving as a flavinylation substrate, we identified a conserved [S/T]GA[S/T] motif within ApbE-associated DUF2271s (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis showing conserved motif and experimental validation

claim: Amantichitinum ursilacus DUF2271 protein is flavinylated in the presence of its cognate ApbE
source: We expressed the Amantichitinum ursilacus DUF2271 protein in Escherichia coli and found that it was flavinylated in the presence of its cognate ApbE (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct experimental evidence from protein expression and purification showing UV fluorescence characteristic of flavin

claim: Replacing the threonine at the predicted flavinylation site in DUF2271 with alanine abrogates flavinylation
source: Consistent with the conserved [S/T]GA[S/T] motif representing the sole ApbE target, we found that replacing the threonine at the predicted flavinylation site with an alanine abrogated flavinylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis data showing loss of UV fluorescence in mutant protein

claim: DUF3570 is a novel ApbE substrate that contains two conserved [S/T]GA[S/T] motifs
source: Consistent with DUF3570 serving as a flavinylation substrate, we identified two conserved [S/T]GA[S/T] motifs within ApbE-associated DUF3570s (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and experimental validation

claim: Chlorobium luteolum DUF3570 is flavinylated in the presence of its cognate ApbE
source: Using the coexpression approach described above, we confirmed that the Chlorobium luteolum DUF3570 was flavinylated in the presence of its cognate ApbE (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct experimental evidence from protein expression showing UV fluorescence

claim: Both [S/T]GA[S/T] motifs in DUF3570 are modified by ApbE
source: Consistent with both of the identified [S/T]GA[S/T] motifs being modified, we found that replacing serines with alanines at both predicted flavinylation sites was required to abrogate flavinylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis data showing that double mutation is required to eliminate flavinylation

claim: Including DUF2271 and DUF3570 in the analysis decreased the number of orphan apbE genomes from 17% to 4%
source: Including DUF2271 and DUF3570 within our analyses significantly expanded the number and diversity of predicted ApbE substrates and decreased the number of orphan apbE genomes within the dataset from 17% to 4% (670 total) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Computational analysis showing improved coverage of ApbE-containing genomes

claim: Five putative transmembrane electron transfer apparatuses associated with flavinylation are present in 6183 genomes
source: From these gene clusters, we identified five putative transmembrane electron transfer apparatuses that are present in 6183 genomes, including 3635 of the 6230 genomes that lack a characterized extracytosolic electron transfer system (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Based on genomic context analysis of flavinylation-associated gene clusters

claim: NapH-like proteins are homologous to NapH, the putative quinone-binding subunit of periplasmic nitrate reductase
source: These proteins are homologous to NapH, the putative quinone-binding subunit of periplasmic nitrate reductase, and exhibit a broad phylogenetic distribution (Figure 4A; Brondijk et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on sequence homology and citation to Brondijk et al., 2002

claim: The majority of NapH-like proteins contain an extracytosolic N-terminal FMN-binding domain
source: The majority of NapH-like proteins identified in our analysis contain an extracytosolic N-terminal FMN-binding domain (1926 gene clusters) whereas the remaining ones (539 gene clusters) are in a genomic locus with a second gene that encodes an FMN-binding domain-containing protein.
evidence: Based on domain analysis of identified NapH-like proteins

claim: NapH-like proteins likely receive electrons from a donor that are transferred via iron-sulfur clusters across the membrane
source: These proteins likely receive electrons from a donor (probably a quinol in some cases) that are transferred via the iron-sulfur cluster across the membrane (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from protein domain architecture and homology to characterized systems

claim: Many NapH-like proteins function with respiratory oxidoreductases
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that many NapH-like proteins function with respiratory oxidoreductases.
evidence: Based on multiple observations including characterized examples and gene cluster associations

claim: Previously characterized NapH-like proteins PceC and NosZ have been shown to be flavinylated
source: Previously characterized NapH-like proteins PceC and NosZ have been shown to be flavinylated and are part of gene clusters for organohalide and nitrous oxide reduction, respectively (Figure 1; Buttet et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies

claim: NapH-like gene clusters with extracytosolic nitrite reductase were identified in 133 genomes
source: We also identified NapH-like gene clusters with an extracytosolic nitrite reductase in 133 genomes or an ethanol oxidase in 172 genomes.
evidence: Based on computational analysis of gene cluster composition

claim: NapH-like gene clusters with ethanol oxidase were identified in 172 genomes
source: We also identified NapH-like gene clusters with an extracytosolic nitrite reductase in 133 genomes or an ethanol oxidase in 172 genomes.
evidence: Based on computational analysis of gene cluster composition

claim: NapH-like electron transfer apparatus is modularly employed to facilitate electron transfer to reductases or from oxidases
source: Thus, while the reactions catalyzed by the majority of NapH-like systems remain unknown, this electron transfer apparatus seems to be modularly employed to facilitate electron transfer to reductases or from oxidases (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from the diversity of oxidoreductases associated with NapH-like proteins

claim: NapH-like associations with nirS and exaA evolved independently multiple times
source: This modularity of NapH-oxidoreductase associations is further underscored by a phylogenetic analysis, which suggests that NapH-like associations with nirS and exaA evolved independently multiple times (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis showing polyphyletic distribution of associations

claim: 1797 flavinylation gene clusters in 1468 genomes encode an MsrQ-like protein
source: We identified 1797 flavinylation gene clusters in 1468 genomes that encode an 'MsrQ-like' (Pfam accession PF01794) protein (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational search for MsrQ-like proteins in flavinylation-associated gene clusters

claim: MsrQ-like gene clusters are broadly conserved in Actinobacteria and infrequently identified in other lineages
source: These clusters are broadly conserved in Actinobacteria and are infrequently identified in other lineages (Figure 2 and Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution analysis shown in figures

claim: MsrQ-like proteins are predicted to have six transmembrane helices and two heme-binding sites
source: MsrQ-like proteins are predicted to have six transmembrane helices and two heme-binding sites.
evidence: Based on computational prediction of protein structure features

claim: MsrQ-like proteins are homologous to MsrQ, the quinone-binding subunit of periplasmic methionine sulfoxide reductase
source: MsrQ-like proteins are homologous to MsrQ, the quinone-binding subunit of periplasmic methionine sulfoxide reductase (Gennaris et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on sequence homology and citation to Gennaris et al., 2015

claim: MsrQ-like proteins are distantly related to eukaryotic NADPH oxidase and STEAP iron reductases
source: MsrQ-like proteins are also distantly related to eukaryotic proteins that function in transmembrane electron transfer, including NADPH oxidase and STEAP iron reductases (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on sequence homology analysis and citation to Zhang et al., 2013

claim: 1437 MsrQ-like proteins contain a C-terminal NAD-binding domain
source: MsrQ-like proteins often contain a C-terminal NAD-binding domain (Pfam accession PF00175, 1437 gene clusters).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of MsrQ-like proteins

claim: 31 MsrQ-like gene clusters include an NuoF-like protein
source: In other cases, the MsrQ-like gene clusters include an NuoF-like protein (Pfam accession PF10589﻿, 31 gene clusters), homologous to the NAD-binding subunit of complex I.
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: At least a subset of MsrQ-like proteins likely use NAD(P)H as a cytosolic electron donor
source: At least a subset of MsrQ-like proteins thus likely use NAD(P)H as a cytosolic electron donor (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from presence of NAD-binding domains in MsrQ-like proteins and gene clusters

claim: 153 MsrQ-like gene clusters encode a protein homologous to the eukaryotic ferrous iron transporter VIT1
source: We also identified 153 MsrQ-like gene clusters that encode a protein homologous to the eukaryotic ferrous iron transporter VIT1 (Pfam accession PF01988).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: Some MsrQ-like systems function as assimilatory iron reductases that facilitate iron uptake through VIT1
source: This association suggests that some MsrQ-like systems function as assimilatory iron reductases that facilitate iron uptake through VIT1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from gene cluster association with VIT1 iron transporter

claim: 3220 flavinylation gene clusters in 3040 genomes encode a PepSY-like protein
source: We identified 3220 flavinylation gene clusters in 3040 genomes that encode a PepSY-like (Pfam accessions PF03929 and PF16357) protein (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational search for PepSY-like proteins in flavinylation-associated gene clusters

claim: PepSY-like proteins contain three transmembrane helices
source: PepSY-like proteins contain three transmembrane helices and are broadly distributed throughout Gram-negative bacteria (Figures 2 and 4C).
evidence: Based on computational prediction of transmembrane helices

claim: PepSY-like proteins are broadly distributed throughout Gram-negative bacteria
source: PepSY-like proteins contain three transmembrane helices and are broadly distributed throughout Gram-negative bacteria (Figures 2 and 4C).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution analysis

claim: 2833 PepSY-like gene clusters encode the flavinylation substrate DUF2271
source: PepSY-like gene clusters frequently encode an ApbE enzyme, the flavinylation substrate DUF2271 (Pfam accession PF10029, 2833 clusters), and a secreted DUF4198 (Pfam accession PF10670, 1500 clusters) protein.
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 1500 PepSY-like gene clusters encode a secreted DUF4198 protein
source: PepSY-like gene clusters frequently encode an ApbE enzyme, the flavinylation substrate DUF2271 (Pfam accession PF10029, 2833 clusters), and a secreted DUF4198 (Pfam accession PF10670, 1500 clusters) protein.
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: Vibrio cholerae VciB possesses extracytosolic iron reductase activity
source: The only characterized PepSY-like homolog, Vibrio cholerae VciB (which is not associated with identified flavinylation components), was reported to possess extracytosolic iron reductase activity (Peng and Payne, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study by Peng and Payne, 2017

claim: 1077 PepSY-like genes have a NAD-binding domain
source: We further identified 1077 PepSY-like genes that have a NAD-binding domain (Pfam accession PF00175), suggesting that a subset of these proteins use cytosolic NADH as an electron donor (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of PepSY-like proteins

claim: A subset of PepSY-like proteins use cytosolic NADH as an electron donor
source: We further identified 1077 PepSY-like genes that have a NAD-binding domain (Pfam accession PF00175), suggesting that a subset of these proteins use cytosolic NADH as an electron donor (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inferred from presence of NAD-binding domain

claim: 108 gene clusters contain both PepSY-like and MsrQ-like genes
source: First, a functional connection to MsrQ-like proteins is suggested by our observation that 108 gene clusters contain both PepSY-like and MsrQ-like genes.
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 167 PepSY-like gene clusters contain a VIT1 ferrous iron transporter
source: Second, 167 PepSY-like gene clusters contain a VIT1 (Pfam accession PF01988) ferrous iron transporter (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: PepSY-like gene clusters have been shown to be repressed by Fur in Shewanella oneidensis and Caulobacter crescentus
source: Finally, PepSY-like gene clusters have been shown to be repressed by Fur (the primary transcription regulator that responds to iron limitation) in Shewanella oneidensis and Caulobacter crescentus (da Silva Neto et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Periplasmic reduction has been shown to be important for the uptake of siderophore-bound iron
source: Moreover, in some cases, PepSY-like proteins may be actively involved in the extraction of siderophore-bound iron, as periplasmic reduction has been shown to be important for the uptake of siderophore-bound iron and 231 PepSY-like gene clusters encode a TonB receptor (Pfam accession PF03544) related to well-characterized outer membrane siderophore transporters (Figure 4C; Liu et al., 2018a; Manck et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018a and Manck et al., 2020

claim: 231 PepSY-like gene clusters encode a TonB receptor related to outer membrane siderophore transporters
source: Moreover, in some cases, PepSY-like proteins may be actively involved in the extraction of siderophore-bound iron, as periplasmic reduction has been shown to be important for the uptake of siderophore-bound iron and 231 PepSY-like gene clusters encode a TonB receptor (Pfam accession PF03544) related to well-characterized outer membrane siderophore transporters (Figure 4C; Liu et al., 2018a; Manck et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 285 flavinylation gene clusters in 275 genomes contain a DsbD protein
source: We identified 285 flavinylation gene clusters in 275 genomes that contain a DsbD protein (Pfam accession PF02683) (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational search for DsbD proteins in flavinylation-associated gene clusters

claim: DsbD is a transmembrane protein family that uses cysteine pairs to transfer electrons across the membrane
source: DsbD is part of a well-studied transmembrane protein family that uses cysteine pairs to transfer electrons across the membrane (Krupp et al., 2001; Missiakas et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on DsbD mechanism

claim: DsbD family proteins generally transfer electrons onto extracytosolic thioredoxin-like proteins
source: DsbD family proteins generally transfer electrons onto extracytosolic thioredoxin-like proteins, which in turn use a similar thiol-disulfide exchange chemistry to promote extracytosolic redox-dependent activities, such as oxidative protein folding (Cho and Collet, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho and Collet, 2013

claim: 227 DsbD gene clusters contain the flavinylation substrate DUF3570
source: The DsbD gene clusters identified in our analyses typically include genes for ApbE, the flavinylation substrate DUF3570 (Pfam accession PF12094, 227 clusters), a thioredoxin-like protein (Pfam accession PF13899, 183 clusters), and a DUF4266 protein (Pfam accession PF14086, 221 clusters).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 183 DsbD gene clusters contain a thioredoxin-like protein
source: The DsbD gene clusters identified in our analyses typically include genes for ApbE, the flavinylation substrate DUF3570 (Pfam accession PF12094, 227 clusters), a thioredoxin-like protein (Pfam accession PF13899, 183 clusters), and a DUF4266 protein (Pfam accession PF14086, 221 clusters).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 221 DsbD gene clusters contain a DUF4266 protein
source: The DsbD gene clusters identified in our analyses typically include genes for ApbE, the flavinylation substrate DUF3570 (Pfam accession PF12094, 227 clusters), a thioredoxin-like protein (Pfam accession PF13899, 183 clusters), and a DUF4266 protein (Pfam accession PF14086, 221 clusters).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: DUF4266 is a small secreted protein with a highly conserved C-terminal CXC sequence motif that may undergo redox cycling
source: DUF4266 is a small secreted protein with a highly conserved C-terminal cysteine – (any amino acid) – cysteine (CXC) sequence motif that may undergo redox cycling.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and inference from cysteine motif structure

claim: 316 gene clusters encode ApbE, DUF3570, thioredoxin-like, and DUF4266 but do not colocalize with DsbD
source: We also detected 316 gene clusters that encode ApbE, DUF3570, thioredoxin-like, and DUF4266 but do not colocalize on the genome with DsbD – implying that this system may be more common than is revealed by the DsbD-dependent analysis presented in Figure 2.
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: A hybrid thioredoxin-like/flavinylation-based system receives electrons from DsbD in some bacteria
source: These observations suggest that a hybrid thioredoxin-like/flavinylation-based system receives electrons from DsbD in some bacteria (Figure 4D).
evidence: Inferred from gene cluster composition showing co-occurrence of DsbD, flavinylation, and thioredoxin components

claim: 25 DsbD-associated gene clusters contain a VIT1 ferrous iron transporter
source: While the function of DUF3570-based electron transfer remains uncertain, 25 gene clusters contain a VIT1 ferrous iron transporter and thus may play a role in iron assimilation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 127 flavinylation gene clusters in 127 genomes have evidence of partial NQR or RNF systems
source: We identified 127 flavinylation gene clusters in 127 genomes, primarily from the Actinobacteria and candidate phyla radiation, with evidence of partial NQR or RNF systems (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: NQR and RNF complexes contain a common core apparatus with two transmembrane electron transfer pathways that achieve semicircular electron flow
source: As shown in Figure 1, the NQR and RNF complexes contain a common core apparatus with two transmembrane electron transfer pathways that together achieve a semicircular electron flow (Juárez et al., 2010; Steuber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1

claim: NQR/RNF-like gene clusters encode components associated with a single electron transfer pathway and likely function for unidirectional electron flow
source: NQR/RNF-like gene clusters encode for components associated with a single electron transfer pathway and thus likely function for unidirectional electron flow (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from incomplete gene cluster composition compared to full NQR/RNF systems

claim: NQR/RNF-like gene clusters encode a protein with an N-terminal membrane domain homologous to NqrB/RnfD and a cytosolic C-terminal domain homologous to NqrF
source: NQR/RNF-like gene clusters encode a protein with an N-terminal membrane domain that is homologous to NqrB/RnfD and a cytosolic C-terminal domain homologous to the NAD-binding domain NqrF (Pfam accession PF00175).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of proteins in NQR/RNF-like gene clusters

claim: NqrB/RnfD is flavinylated by ApbE and plays a role in electron transfer across the membrane
source: NqrB/RnfD is flavinylated by ApbE and is thought to play a role in electron transfer across the membrane (Juárez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Juárez et al., 2010

claim: NQR/RNF-like systems presumably use NAD(P)H as a cytosolic electron donor
source: This system presumably uses NAD(P)H as a cytosolic electron donor for electron transfer to an extracytosolic FMN-binding domain.
evidence: Inferred from presence of NAD-binding domain in the protein

claim: Six NQR/RNF-like gene clusters contain a VIT1 ferrous iron transporter
source: Six NQR/RNF-like gene clusters contain a VIT1 ferrous iron transporter, suggesting that some of these systems function in iron assimilation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: 260 P19 gene clusters, mostly in Gram-positive bacteria, contain a gene with an FMN-binding domain
source: We identified 260 P19 gene clusters, mostly in Gram-positive bacteria, that contain a gene with an FMN-binding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: Many Gram-negative P19 gene clusters lack an FMN-binding gene but contain an additional thioredoxin-like gene
source: Interestingly, many Gram-negative P19 gene clusters lack an FMN-binding gene but contain an additional thioredoxin-like gene (Liu et al., 2018b; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis and citation to Liu et al., 2018b

claim: A gene cluster that includes P19 and FTR1 iron transporter has been shown to encode a system involved in iron assimilation
source: A gene cluster that includes the ferrous iron-binding protein P19 (Pfam accession PF10634) and the FTR1 (Pfam accession PF03239) iron transporter has previously been shown to encode a mechanistically uncharacterized system involved in iron assimilation (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2010

claim: Fumarate reductase-like enzymes often contain an FMN-binding domain
source: We observe that fumarate reductase-like enzymes often contain an FMN-binding domain (3070 proteins encoded by 2979 distinct gene clusters in 1236 genomes) or are part of gene clusters (±2 genes) that contain an FMN-binding domain (189 gene clusters in 171 genomes) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on domain analysis and gene cluster composition

claim: Several characterized fumarate reductase-like enzymes are extracytosolic and function in respiration
source: Several characterized fumarate reductase-like enzymes (including fumarate, urocanate, and methacrylate reductases) are extracytosolic and function in respiration (Bogachev et al., 2012; Light et al., 2019; Mikoulinskaia et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies

claim: Listeria monocytogenes fumarate reductase has been shown to be flavinylated
source: The Listeria monocytogenes fumarate reductase and the S. oneidensis urocanate reductase have been shown to be flavinylated (Bogachev et al., 2012; Light et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Shewanella oneidensis urocanate reductase has been shown to be flavinylated
source: The Listeria monocytogenes fumarate reductase and the S. oneidensis urocanate reductase have been shown to be flavinylated (Bogachev et al., 2012; Light et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: In flavinylated fumarate and urocanate reductases, the flavinylation motif facilitates electron transfer from electron transport chain components to the enzyme active site
source: In both cases, the flavinylation motif is thought to facilitate electron transfer from electron transport chain components encoded elsewhere on the genome to the enzyme active site (Kees et al., 2019; Light et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kees et al., 2019 and Light et al., 2019

claim: FMN-binding domains mediate electron transfer from membrane components to a prevalent class of extracytosolic reductases
source: These observations thus suggest that FMN-binding domains mediate electron transfer from membrane components to a prevalent class of extracytosolic reductases and highlight another connection between flavinylation and respiration.
evidence: Inferred from the widespread association of FMN-binding domains with fumarate reductase-like enzymes

claim: Cytochrome and flavinylated electron transfer components appear to perform similar electron transfer roles within related systems
source: A comparison of extracytosolic electron transfer systems identified in our analyses revealed multiple instances in which cytochrome and flavinylated electron transfer components appear to be performing similar electron transfer roles within related systems.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of gene clusters and protein domain architectures

claim: The extracytosolic Shewanella oneidensis fumarate reductase contains an N-terminal multi-heme cytochrome c domain
source: The extracytosolic S. oneidensis fumarate reductase contains an N-terminal multi-heme cytochrome c domain (Pfam accession PF14537), whereas the related L. monocytogenes enzyme uses an FMN-binding domain to connect to the electron transport chain (Figure 5B; DiChristina and DeLong, 1994; Light et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to DiChristina and DeLong, 1994 and Light et al., 2019, and reference to Figure 5B

claim: The Listeria monocytogenes fumarate reductase uses an FMN-binding domain to connect to the electron transport chain
source: The extracytosolic S. oneidensis fumarate reductase contains an N-terminal multi-heme cytochrome c domain (Pfam accession PF14537), whereas the related L. monocytogenes enzyme uses an FMN-binding domain to connect to the electron transport chain (Figure 5B; DiChristina and DeLong, 1994; Light et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to DiChristina and DeLong, 1994 and Light et al., 2019, and reference to Figure 5B

claim: Different microbes utilize flavinylation and cytochrome domains in a similar fashion to link respiratory enzymes to electron transport chains
source: Different microbes thus seem to utilize flavinylation and cytochrome domains in a similar fashion to link respiratory enzymes to electron transport chains.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of fumarate reductases with different electron transfer domains

claim: 147 gene clusters within 108 genomes encode separate fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome proteins
source: We identified 147 gene clusters within 108 genomes that encode separate fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome proteins and 879 genes within 360 genomes that encode a single protein with both fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome domains (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on gene cluster and domain architecture analysis

claim: 879 genes within 360 genomes encode a single protein with both fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome domains
source: We identified 147 gene clusters within 108 genomes that encode separate fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome proteins and 879 genes within 360 genomes that encode a single protein with both fumarate reductase-like and cytochrome domains (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on gene cluster and domain architecture analysis

claim: 99 genomes encode both cytochrome- and flavinylation-associated fumarate reductase-like enzymes
source: Many genomes encode multiple fumarate reductase-like paralogs and 99 genomes encode both cytochrome- and flavinylation-associated enzymes (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on genome-wide analysis of fumarate reductase-like enzyme distribution

claim: Shewanella oneidensis contains a flavinylated urocanate reductase that exhibits a respiratory function
source: This dynamic is exemplified by S. oneidensis, which in addition to the mentioned cytochrome-associated fumarate reductase contains a flavinylated urocanate reductase that also exhibits a respiratory function (Figure 5C; Bogachev et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bogachev et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 5C

claim: Flavinylation- and cytochrome-based extracytosolic electron transfer mechanisms coexist within some microbes
source: Broadly similar flavinylation- and cytochrome-based extracytosolic electron transfer mechanisms thus seemingly coexist within some microbes.
evidence: Inferred from observation that some genomes encode both types of systems

claim: Multi-heme cytochromes bind multiple hemes to achieve longer distance extracytosolic electron transfer
source: Multi-heme cytochromes are proteins that bind multiple hemes to achieve longer distance extracytosolic electron transfer (Blumberger, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blumberger, 2018

claim: Extracytosolic proteins with multiple FMN-binding domains are common, with 2081 proteins in 1530 genomes
source: We have observed that extracytosolic proteins with multiple FMN-binding domains are also common (2081 proteins in 1530 genomes), particularly in Gram-positive bacteria, and contain as many as 13 predicted flavinylation sites (Figure 6A and B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of proteins with multiple FMN-binding domains

claim: Multi-flavinylated proteins are particularly common in Gram-positive bacteria
source: We have observed that extracytosolic proteins with multiple FMN-binding domains are also common (2081 proteins in 1530 genomes), particularly in Gram-positive bacteria, and contain as many as 13 predicted flavinylation sites (Figure 6A and B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Some multi-flavinylated proteins contain as many as 13 predicted flavinylation sites
source: We have observed that extracytosolic proteins with multiple FMN-binding domains are also common (2081 proteins in 1530 genomes), particularly in Gram-positive bacteria, and contain as many as 13 predicted flavinylation sites (Figure 6A and B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on domain analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Multi-flavinylated proteins are often associated with established transmembrane electron transfer components
source: We find that multi-flavinylated proteins are often associated with established transmembrane electron transfer components and thus likely receive electrons through conventional mechanisms (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Some multi-flavinylated protein gene clusters contain large unannotated proteins with putative cell wall-binding domains
source: We observe that some clusters contain large unannotated proteins with putative cell wall-binding domains – such as SLH (Pfam accession PF00395), Rib (Pfam accession PF08428), FIVAR (Pfam accession PF07554), or LysM (Pfam accession PF01476) – and are thus likely involved in redox chemistry within the cell wall or at the cell surface (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of proteins in multi-flavinylated gene clusters

claim: Some multi-flavinylated proteins are likely involved in redox chemistry within the cell wall or at the cell surface
source: We observe that some clusters contain large unannotated proteins with putative cell wall-binding domains – such as SLH (Pfam accession PF00395), Rib (Pfam accession PF08428), FIVAR (Pfam accession PF07554), or LysM (Pfam accession PF01476) – and are thus likely involved in redox chemistry within the cell wall or at the cell surface (Figure 6D).
evidence: Inferred from presence of cell wall-binding domains

claim: 157 multi-flavinylated protein gene clusters encode additional proteins with FMN-binding domains
source: We also identified 157 clusters that encode a multi-flavinylated protein and additional proteins with FMN-binding domains (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis

claim: Some multi-flavinylated protein gene clusters encode as many as five proteins with FMN-binding domains
source: These clusters encode as many as five proteins with FMN-binding domains and frequently contain multiple multi-flavinylated proteins (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on gene cluster composition analysis shown in Figure 6D and E

claim: Some multi-flavinylated proteins are part of multi-step electron transfer pathways and may form elaborate multi-subunit complexes that span the cell wall
source: These observations suggest that some multi-flavinylated proteins are part of multi-step electron transfer pathways and may form elaborate multi-subunit complexes that span the cell wall.
evidence: Inferred from gene cluster composition showing multiple FMN-binding proteins

claim: A subset of multi-flavinylated gene clusters encode proteins with multiple fumarate reductase-like domains that likely establish an unusual multi-functional reductase platform
source: We identified a subset of clusters that encode proteins with multiple fumarate reductase-like domains that likely establish an unusual multi-functional reductase platform (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: Inferred from domain architecture analysis

claim: A number of RNF clusters contain multi-flavinylated RnfGs
source: We also identified a number of RNF clusters that contain multi-flavinylated RnfGs (the extracytosolic flavinylated subunit in RNF complexes) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on domain analysis of RnfG proteins in RNF gene clusters

claim: Multi-flavinylated RNF complexes likely provide a second electron transfer pathway that facilitates transfer to alternative extracytosolic acceptors
source: These multi-flavinylated RNF complexes likely provide a second electron transfer pathway that facilitates transfer to alternative extracytosolic acceptors.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of multiple flavinylation sites in RnfG

claim: Multi-flavinylated RNF bifurcated electron transfer would be similar to a multi-heme cytochrome-based transfer mechanism suggested in studies of a methanogen RNF
source: This type of bifurcated electron transfer would be similar to a multi-heme cytochrome-based transfer mechanism recently suggested in studies of a methanogen RNF (Holmes et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holmes et al., 2019

claim: A subset of multi-flavinylated RnfGs in the family Christensenellales contain a multi-heme cytochrome domain
source: Interestingly, we also identified a subset of multi-flavinylated RnfGs in the family Christensenellales that contain a multi-heme cytochrome domain and thus may assume additional functions relevant for cytochrome-based electron transfer (Figure 6H).
evidence: Based on domain architecture analysis

claim: ApbE-mediated flavinylation is a prominent feature of bacterial physiology
source: Our large-scale survey of diverse genomes extends this approach and reveals that ApbE-mediated flavinylation is a prominent feature of bacterial physiology.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive genomic analysis showing widespread distribution

claim: Modular properties facilitate the integration of flavinylated components with various biochemical processes
source: More granular analyses of gene clusters provide evidence consistent with extracytosolic flavinylation usage in diverse redox activities and suggest that modular properties facilitate the integration of flavinylated components with various biochemical processes.
evidence: Inferred from observation of diverse gene cluster associations and phylogenetic patterns

claim: ApbE-flavinylated proteins represent a third major class of mediators of extracytosolic electron transfer alongside thioredoxin-like proteins and cytochromes
source: Our findings suggest that, alongside thioredoxin-like proteins and cytochromes, ApbE-flavinylated proteins represent a third major class of mediators of extracytosolic electron transfer.
evidence: Inferred from the widespread distribution and diverse functions of flavinylated proteins

claim: The ApbE-catalyzed phosphoester linkage is outside the flavin's isoalloxazine ring and unlikely to impact the cofactor's redox potential
source: By contrast, the ApbE-catalyzed phosphoester linkage is outside the flavin's isoalloxazine ring and unlikely to impact the cofactor's redox potential.
evidence: Based on chemical structure knowledge and comparison to other flavinylation types

claim: Non-flavinylated FMN-binding domains have low flavin-binding affinity
source: Since non-flavinylated FMN-binding domains have low flavin-binding affinity, the ApbE-catalyzed reaction may simply function to secure the cofactor to the protein (Borshchevskiy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Borshchevskiy et al., 2015

claim: Interactions with the folded protein stabilize the flavin's semiquinone state in a fashion that presumably enhances electron transfer
source: Once the flavin is linked to the FMN-binding domain, interactions with the folded protein stabilize the flavin's semiquinone state in a fashion that presumably enhances electron transfer (Barquera, 2014; Backiel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barquera, 2014 and Backiel et al., 2008

claim: The NQR complex is a cation-pumping NADH:quinone oxidoreductase
source: These systems include the cation-pumping NADH:quinone oxidoreductase (NQR) and Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation (RNF) complexes (Figure 1B and C)
evidence: Established knowledge about characterized systems, supported by Figure 1B

claim: The RNF complex is the Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation complex
source: These systems include the cation-pumping NADH:quinone oxidoreductase (NQR) and Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation (RNF) complexes (Figure 1B and C)
evidence: Established knowledge about characterized systems, supported by Figure 1C

claim: NQR and RNF complexes are widely distributed throughout microbial life
source: These systems are widely distributed throughout microbial life and catalyze key intermediate steps in the energy metabolism of numerous microbes (Barquera, 2014; Buckel and Thauer, 2018; Reyes-Prieto et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barquera, 2014; Buckel and Thauer, 2018; Reyes-Prieto et al., 2014

claim: NQR and RNF complexes catalyze key intermediate steps in the energy metabolism of numerous microbes
source: These systems are widely distributed throughout microbial life and catalyze key intermediate steps in the energy metabolism of numerous microbes (Barquera, 2014; Buckel and Thauer, 2018; Reyes-Prieto et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barquera, 2014; Buckel and Thauer, 2018; Reyes-Prieto et al., 2014

claim: Flavinylation-based electron transfer mechanisms might be particularly advantageous within iron-poor environments
source: Based on this precedent, it seems plausible that flavinylation-based electron transfer mechanisms might be particularly advantageous within iron-poor environments.
evidence: Speculative inference based on analogy to ferredoxin/flavodoxin relationship

claim: The coexistence of functionally similar but mechanistically distinctive flavinylation and cytochrome electron transfer components may reflect divergent resource management strategies in distinct environmental contexts
source: The coexistence of functionally similar but mechanistically distinctive flavinylation and cytochrome electron transfer components may thus, in part, reflect divergent resource management strategies in distinct environmental contexts.
evidence: Speculative inference about evolutionary and ecological factors

claim: Multi-heme cytochromes can establish 'nanowires' that have potential biotechnological applications
source: A particularly noteworthy aspect of multi-heme cytochromes concerns their ability to establish 'nanowires' that have a variety of potential biotechnological applications (Blumberger, 2018; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blumberger, 2018 and Liu et al., 2020

claim: The electron-transferring behavior of multi-flavinylated proteins may provide an interesting juxtaposition to multi-heme cytochromes with implications for novel redox-based biotechnologies
source: Considering the unique redox properties of flavins, the electron-transferring behavior of multi-flavinylated proteins may provide an interesting juxtaposition to multi-heme cytochromes with implications for the development of novel redox-based biotechnologies.
evidence: Speculative inference about potential applications

claim: 18,965 bacterial genomes and 238 archaeal genomes encode an FMN-binding domain-containing protein and/or an ApbE enzyme
source: We found that 18,965 of bacterial genomes and 238 of archaeal genomes encode an FMN-binding domain-containing protein and/or an ApbE enzyme.
evidence: Based on computational search of 31,910 prokaryotic genomes

claim: 8928 genomes contain characterized extracytosolic electron transfer systems
source: These analyses revealed characterized systems in 8928 genomes broadly distributed across bacterial life (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on operational definitions applied to gene cluster analysis

claim: 6230 genomes contain evidence of extracytosolic flavinylation but lack a characterized extracytosolic electron transfer system
source: In addition to assigning extracytosolic electron transfer functions, our analyses identified 6230 genomes that contained evidence of extracytosolic flavinylation but lacked a characterized extracytosolic electron transfer system.
evidence: Based on computational analysis comparing genomes with flavinylation components to those with characterized systems

claim: Many genomes have multiple ApbE and/or FMN-binding genes and likely possess multiple extracytosolic electron transfer functions
source: We also found that many genomes have multiple ApbE and/or FMN-binding genes and thus likely possess multiple extracytosolic electron transfer functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on counting genes per genome and inference about functional implications

claim: 17% of genomes with flavinylation components encode an ApbE but no FMN-binding domain-containing protein
source: However, preliminary analyses identified 17% of genomes (2571 total) within our dataset that encoded an ApbE but no FMN-binding domain-containing protein – implying that some ApbE substrates lack an FMN-binding domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on computational analysis of domain composition

claim: In some genomes a single gene encodes a protein with both ApbE and DUF2271 domains
source: In some genomes a single gene encodes a protein with both ApbE and DUF2271 domains (e.g., NCBI accession RUL87804.1), but more commonly a separate DUF2271 gene is part of a gene cluster that includes an apbE.
evidence: Based on gene and domain architecture analysis with specific example

claim: 2465 flavinylation gene clusters in 2153 genomes encode a NapH-like iron-sulfur cluster-binding protein
source: We identified 2465 flavinylation gene clusters in 2153 genomes that encode an 'NapH-like' iron-sulfur cluster-binding protein (Pfam accession PF12801 or KEGG accession K19339) that contains several transmembrane helices (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on computational search and domain analysis

claim: Previously characterized NapH-like systems were identified within 1197 genomes
source: These previously characterized NapH-like systems were identified within 1197 genomes within our dataset (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on application of operational definitions to identify characterized systems

claim: Microbes switch from ferredoxin to flavodoxin usage in iron-poor environments to conserve cellular iron reserves
source: Microbes switch from ferredoxin to flavodoxin usage in iron-poor environments – presumably because minimizing the demand for iron cofactors is important for conserving the cellular iron reserve in this context (Knight et al., 1966; Smillie, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knight et al., 1966 and Smillie, 1965
